entries.1958f85b4f13145ad896f9759573ff7afc8a1374: <div sID="gen17352" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Jer.8" sID="Jer.8"/> <div eID="gen17352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17353" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17354" type="x-p"/> The prophet proceeds, in this chapter, both to magnify and to justify the destruction that God was bringing upon this people, to show how grievous it would be and yet how righteous. I. He represents the judgments coming as so very terrible that death should appear so as most to be dreaded and yet should be desired, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.1-Jer.8.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He aggravates the wretched stupidity and wilfulness of this people as that which brought this ruin upon them, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4-Jer.8.12">ver. 4-12</reference>. III. He describes the great confusion and consternation that the whole land should be in upon the alarm of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.13-Jer.8.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. IV. The prophet is himself deeply affected with it and lays it very much to heart, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18-Jer.8.22">ver. 18-22</reference>.
entries.c6f308bff63f543fa695bba4c38bef81dbf3fe52: <div eID="gen17354" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17353" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Indignities Threatened to the Dead. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17355" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> At that time, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , they shall bring out the bones of the kings of Judah, and the bones of his princes, and the bones of the priests, and the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, out of their graves: <hi type="super">2</hi> And they shall spread them before the sun, and the moon, and all the host of heaven, whom they have loved, and whom they have served, and after whom they have walked, and whom they have sought, and whom they have worshipped: they shall not be gathered, nor be buried; they shall be for dung upon the face of the earth. <hi type="super">3</hi> And death shall be chosen rather than life by all the residue of them that remain of this evil family, which remain in all the places whither I have driven them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen17355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17356" type="x-p"/> These verses might fitly have been joined to the close of the foregoing chapter, as giving a further description of the dreadful desolation which the army of the Chaldeans should make in the land. It shall strangely alter the property of death itself, and for the worse too. <div eID="gen17356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17357" type="x-p"/> I. Death shall not now be, as it always used to be—the repose of the dead. When Job makes his court to the grave it is in hope of this, that <hi type="italic">there he shall rest with kings and counsellors of the earth;</hi> but now the ashes of the dead, even of <hi type="italic">kings</hi> and <hi type="italic">princes,</hi> shall be disturbed, and their <hi type="italic">bones scattered at the grave's mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.141.7">Ps. cxli. 7</reference>. It was threatened in the close of the former chapter that the slain should be unburied; that might be through neglect, and was not so strange; but here we find the graves of those that were buried industriously and maliciously opened by the victorious enemy, who either for covetousness, hoping to find treasure in the graves, or for spite to the nation and in a rage against it, <hi type="italic">brought out the bones of the kings of Judah and the princes.</hi> The dignity of their sepulchres could not secure them, nay, did the more expose them to be rifled; but it was base and barbarous thus to trample upon royal dust. We will hope that the bones of good Josiah were not disturbed, because he piously protected the bones of the man of God when he burnt the bones of the idolatrous priests, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.18">2 Kings xxiii. 18</reference>. The bones of the priests and prophets too were digged up and thrown about. Some think the false prophets and the idol-priests, God putting this mark of ignominy upon them: but, if they were God's prophets and his priests, it is what the Psalmist complains of as the fruit of the outrage of the enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1-Ps.79.2">Ps. lxxix. 1, 2</reference>. Nay, those of the spiteful Chaldeans that could not reach to violate the sepulchres of princes and priests would rather play at small game than sit out, and therefore pulled the bones of the ordinary <hi type="italic">inhabitants of Jerusalem out of their graves.</hi> The barbarous nations were sometimes guilty of these absurd and inhuman triumphs over those they had conquered, and God permitted it here, for a mark of his displeasure against the generation of his wrath, and for terror to those that survived. The bones, being dug out of the graves, were spread abroad upon the face of the earth in contempt, and to make the reproach the more spreading and lasting. They spread them to be dried that they might carry them about in triumph, or might make fuel of them, or make some superstitious use of them. <hi type="italic">They shall be spread before the sun</hi> (for they shall not be ashamed openly to avow the fact at noon day) and before <hi type="italic">the moon and</hi> stars, even <hi type="italic">all the host of heaven,</hi> whom they have made idols of, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">v. 2</reference>. From the mention of the <hi type="italic">sun, moon, and stars,</hi> which should be the unconcerned spectators of this tragedy, the prophet takes occasion to show how they had idolized them, and paid those respects to them which they should have paid to God only, that it might be observed how little they got by worshipping the creature, for the creatures they worshipped when they were in distress saw it, but regarded it not, nor gave them any relief, but were rather pleased to see those abused in being vilified by whom they had been abused in being deified. See how their respects to their idols are enumerated, to show how we ought to behave towards our God. 1. They <hi type="italic">loved</hi> them. As amiable being and bountiful benefactors they esteemed them and delighted in them, and therefore did all that follows. 2. They <hi type="italic">served</hi> them, did all they could in honour of them, and thought nothing too much; they conformed to all the laws of their superstition, without disputing. 3. They <hi type="italic">walked after</hi> them, strove to imitate and resemble them, according to the characters and accounts of them they had received, which gave rise and countenance to much of the abominable wickedness of the heathen. 4. They <hi type="italic">sought</hi> them, consulted them as oracles, appealed to them as judges, implored their favour, and prayed to them as their benefactors. 5. They <hi type="italic">worshipped</hi> them, gave them divine honour, as having a sovereign dominion over them. Before these light of heaven, which they had courted, shall their dead bodies be cast, and left to putrefy, and to be <hi type="italic">as dung upon the face of the earth;</hi> and the sun's shining upon them will but make them the more noisome and offensive. Whatever we make a god of but the true God only, it will stand us in no stead on the other side death and the grave, nor for the body, much less for the soul. <div eID="gen17357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17358" type="x-p"/> II. Death shall now be what it never used to be—the choice of the living, not because there appears in it any thing delightsome; on the contrary, death never appeared in more horrid frightful shapes than now, when they cannot promise themselves either a comfortable death or a human burial; and yet every thing in this world shall become so irksome, and all the prospects so black and dismal, that <hi type="italic">death shall be chosen rather than life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.3">v. 3</reference>), not in a believing hope of happiness in the other life, but in an utter despair of any ease in this life. The nation is now reduced to a <hi type="italic">family,</hi> so small is <hi type="italic">the residue of those that remain</hi> in it; and it is an <hi type="italic">evil family,</hi> still as bad as ever, their hearts unhumbled and their lusts unmortified. These <hi type="italic">remain</hi> alive (and that is all) in the many <hi type="italic">places whither they were driven</hi> by the judgments of God, some prisoners in the country of their enemies, others beggars in their neighbour's country, and others fugitives and vagabonds there and in their own country. And, though those that died died very miserably, yet those that survived and were thus driven out should live yet more miserably, so that they should <hi type="italic">choose death rather than life,</hi> and wish a thousand times that they had fallen with those that fell by the sword. Let this cure us of the inordinate love of life, that the case may be such that it may become a burden and terror, and we may be strongly tempted to <hi type="italic">choose strangling</hi> and death rather.
entries.c08779347e58e1d70e5bf4db9b6adb739ec3f32a: <div eID="gen17358" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Full of Impenitent Sinners; Hardened Wickedness of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17359" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Moreover thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Shall they fall, and not arise? shall he turn away, and not return? <hi type="super">5</hi> Why <hi type="italic">then</hi> is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return. <hi type="super">6</hi> I hearkened and heard, <hi type="italic">but</hi> they spake not aright: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle. <hi type="super">7</hi> Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> How do ye say, We <hi type="italic">are</hi> wise, and the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he <hi type="italic">it;</hi> the pen of the scribes <hi type="italic">is</hi> in vain. <hi type="super">9</hi> The wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> are ashamed, they are dismayed and taken: lo, they have rejected the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and what wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> in them? <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore will I give their wives unto others, <hi type="italic">and</hi> their fields to them that shall inherit <hi type="italic">them:</hi> for every one from the least even unto the greatest is given to covetousness, from the prophet even unto the priest every one dealeth falsely. <hi type="super">11</hi> For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no peace. <hi type="super">12</hi> Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore shall they fall among them that fall: in the time of their visitation they shall be cast down, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17360" type="x-p"/> The prophet here is instructed to set before this people the folly of their impenitence, which was it that brought this ruin upon them. They are here represented as the most stupid senseless people in the world, that would not be made wise by all the methods that Infinite Wisdom took to bring them to themselves and their right mind, and so to prevent the ruin that was coming upon them. <div eID="gen17360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17361" type="x-p"/> I. They would not attend to the dictates of reason. They would not act in the affairs of their souls with the same common prudence with which they acted in other things. Sinners would become saints if they would but show themselves men, and religion would soon rule them if right reason might. Observe it here. <hi type="italic">Come, and let us reason together, saith the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.4-Jer.8.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Shall men fall and not arise?</hi> If men happen to fall to the ground, to fall into the dirt, will they not get up again as fast as they can? They are not such fools as to lie still when they are down. Shall <hi type="italic">a man turn aside</hi> out of the right way? Yes, the most careful traveller may miss his way; but then, as soon as he is aware of it, <hi type="italic">will he not return?</hi> Yes, certainly he will, with all speed, and will thank him that showed him his mistake. Thus men do in other things. <hi type="italic">Why then has this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding?</hi> Why do not they, when they have fallen into sin, hasten to get up again by repentance? Why do not they, when they see they have missed their way, correct their error and reform? No man in his wits will go on in a way that he knows will never bring him to his journey's end; <hi type="italic">why then has this people slidden back by a perpetual backsliding?</hi> See the nature of sin—it is a <hi type="italic">backsliding</hi> it is going back from the right way, not only into a by-path, but into a contrary path, back from the way that leads to life to that which leads to utter destruction. And this backsliding, if almighty grace do not interpose to prevent it, will be a perpetual backsliding. The sinner not only wanders endlessly, but proceeds end-ways towards ruin. The same subtlety of the tempter that brings men to sin holds them fast in it, and they contribute to their own captivity: <hi type="italic">They hold fast deceit.</hi> Sin is a great cheat, and they <hi type="italic">hold it fast;</hi> they love it dearly, and resolve to stick to it, and baffle all the methods God takes to separate between them and their sins. The excuses they make for their sins are deceits, and so are all their hopes of impunity; yet they hold fast these, and will not be undeceived, and therefore <hi type="italic">they refuse to return.</hi> Note, There is some deceit or other which those hold fast that go on wilfully in sinful ways, some <hi type="italic">lie in their right hand,</hi> by which they keep hold of their sins. <div eID="gen17361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17362" type="x-p"/> II. They would not attend to the dictates of conscience, which is our reason reflecting upon ourselves and our own actions, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">v. 6</reference>. Observe, 1. What expectations there were from them, that they would bethink themselves: <hi type="italic">I hearkened and heard.</hi> The prophet listened to see what effect his preaching had upon them; God himself listened, as one that desires not the death of sinners, that would have been glad to hear any thing that promised repentance, that would certainly have heard it if there had been any thing said of that tendency, and would soon have answered it with comfort, as he did David when he said, <hi type="italic">I will confess,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">Ps. xxxii. 5</reference>. God <hi type="italic">looks upon men</hi> when they have done amiss (<reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job xxxiii. 27</reference>), to see what they will do next; he <hi type="italic">hearkens and hears.</hi> 2. How these expectations were disappointed: <hi type="italic">They spoke not aright,</hi> as I thought they would have done. They did not only not <hi type="italic">do right,</hi> but not so much as <hi type="italic">speak right;</hi> God could not get a good word from them, nothing on which to ground any favour to them or hopes concerning them. There was <hi type="italic">none of them</hi> that <hi type="italic">spoke aright,</hi> none that <hi type="italic">repented him of his wickedness.</hi> those that have sinned then, and then only, speak aright when they speak of repenting; and it is sad when those that have made so much work for repentance do not say a word of repenting. Not only did God not find any repenting of the national wickedness, which might have helped to empty the measure of public guilt, but none repented of that particular wickedness which he knew himself guilty of. (1.) They did not so much as take the first step towards repentance; they did not so much as say, <hi type="italic">What have I done?</hi> There was no motion towards it, not the least sign or token of it. Note, True repentance beings in a serious and impartial inquiry into ourselves, <hi type="italic">what have we done,</hi> arising from a conviction that we have done amiss. (2.) They were so far from repenting of their sins that they went on resolutely in their sins: <hi type="italic">Every one turned to his course,</hi> his wicked course, that course of sin which he had chosen and accustomed himself to, <hi type="italic">as the horse rushes into the battle,</hi> eager upon action, and scorning to be curbed. How the horse rushes into the battle is elegantly described, <reference osisRef="Job.39.21">Job xxxix. 21</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">He mocks at fear and is not affrighted.</hi> Thus the daring sinner laughs at the threatenings of the word as bugbears, and runs violently upon the instruments of death and slaughter, and nothing will be restrained from him. <div eID="gen17362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17363" type="x-p"/> III. They would not attend to the dictates of providence, nor understand the voice of God in them, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">v. 7</reference>. It is an instance of their sottishness that, though they are God's people, and therefore should readily understand his mind upon every intimation of it, yet they <hi type="italic">know not the judgment of the Lord;</hi> they apprehend not the meaning either of a mercy or an affliction, not how to accommodate themselves to either, nor to answer God's intention in either. They know not how to improve the seasons of grave that God affords them when he sends them his prophets, nor how to make use of the rebukes they are under when <hi type="italic">his voice cries in the city.</hi> They <hi type="italic">discern not the signs of the times</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.3">Matt. xvi. 3</reference>), nor are aware how God is dealing with them. They know not that way of duty which God had prescribed them, though it be written both in their hearts and in their books. 2. It is an aggravation of their sottishness that there is so much sagacity in the inferior creatures. <hi type="italic">The stork in the heaven knows her appointed times</hi> of coming and continuing; so do other season-birds, <hi type="italic">the turtle, the crane, and the swallow.</hi> These by a natural instinct change their quarters, as the temper of the air alters; they come when the spring comes, and go, we know not whither, when the winter approaches, probably into warmer climates, as some birds come with winter and go when that is over. <div eID="gen17363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17364" type="x-p"/> IV. They would not attend to the dictates of the written word. They say, <hi type="italic">We are wise;</hi> but <hi type="italic">how</hi> can they say so? <reference osisRef="Jer.8.8">v. 8</reference>. With what face can they pretend to any thing of wisdom, when they do not understand themselves so well as the brute-creatures? Why, truly, they think they are wise because <hi type="italic">the law of the Lord is with them,</hi> the book of the law and the interpreters of it; and their neighbours, for the same reason, conclude they are wise, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deut. iv. 6</reference>. But their pretensions are groundless for all this: <hi type="italic">Lo, certainly in vain made he it;</hi> surely never any people had Bibles to so little purpose as they have. They might as well have been without the law, unless they had made a better use of it. God has indeed made it able to make men wise to salvation, but as to them it is made so in vain, for they are never the wiser for it: <hi type="italic">The pen of the scribes,</hi> of those that first wrote the law and of those that now write expositions of it, <hi type="italic">is in vain.</hi> Both the favour of their God and the labour of their scribes are lost upon them; they receive the grace of God therein in vain. Note, There are many that enjoy abundance of the means of grace, that have great plenty of Bibles and ministers, but they have them in vain; they do not answer the end of their having them. But it might be said, They have some wise men among them, to whom the law and the pen of the scribes are not in vain. To this it is answered (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The wise men are ashamed,</hi> that is, they have reasons to be so, that they have not made a better use of their wisdom, and lived more up to it. <hi type="italic">They are confounded and taken;</hi> all their wisdom has not served to keep them from those courses that tend to their ruin. They are taken in the same snares that others of their neighbours, who have not pretended to so much wisdom, are taken in, and filled with the same confusion. Those that have more knowledge than others, and yet do no better than others for their own souls, have reason to be ashamed. They talk of their wisdom, but, <hi type="italic">Lo, they have rejected the word of the Lord;</hi> they would not be governed by it, would not follow its direction, would not do what they knew; <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">what wisdom is in them?</hi> None to any purpose; none that will be found to their praise at the great day, how much soever it is found to their pride now. The pretenders to wisdom, who said, "<hi type="italic">We are wise and the law of the Lord is with us,</hi>" were the priests and the false prophets; with them the prophet here deals plainly. 1. He threatens the judgments of God against them. Their families and estates shall be ruined (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their wives shall be given to others,</hi> when they are taken captives, <hi type="italic">and their fields</hi> shall be taken from them by their victorious enemy and shall be given <hi type="italic">to those that shall inherit them,</hi> not only strip them for once, but take possession of them as their own and acquire a property in them as their own and acquire a property in them, which they shall transmit to their posterity. And (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.12">v. 12</reference>), notwithstanding all their pretensions to wisdom and sanctity, <hi type="italic">they shall fall among those that fall;</hi> for, <hi type="italic">if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall together into the ditch. In the time of their visitation,</hi> when the wickedness of the land comes to be enquired into, it will be found that they have contributed to it more than any, and therefore <hi type="italic">they shall be</hi> sure to be <hi type="italic">cast down</hi> and cast out. 2. He gives a reason for these judgments (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.10-Jer.8.12">v. 10-12</reference>), even the same account of their badness which we meet with before (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.13-Jer.6.15">ch. vi. 13-15</reference>), where it was opened at large. (1.) They were greedy of the wealth of this world, which is bad enough in any, but worst in prophets and priests, who should be best acquainted with another world and therefore should be most dead to this. But these, <hi type="italic">from the least to the greatest,</hi> were <hi type="italic">given to covetousness.</hi> The <hi type="italic">priests teach for hire</hi> and the <hi type="italic">prophets divine for money,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mic. iii. 11</reference>. (2.) They made no conscience of speaking truth, no, not when they spoke as priests and prophets: <hi type="italic">Every one deals falsely,</hi> looks one way and rows another. There is no such thing as sincerity among them. (3.) They flattered people in their sins, and so flattered them into destruction. They pretended to be the physicians of the state, but knew not how to apply proper remedies to its growing maladies; they <hi type="italic">healed them slightly,</hi> killed the patient with palliative cures, silencing their fears and complaints with, "<hi type="italic">Peace, peace,</hi> all is well, and there is no danger," when the God of heaven was proceeding in his controversy with them, so that there could be no peace to them. (4.) When it was made to appear how basely they prevaricated <hi type="italic">they</hi> were not at all ashamed of it, but rather gloried in it, (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">They could not blush,</hi> so perfectly lost were they to all sense of virtue and honour. When they were convicted of the grossest forgeries they would justify what they had done, and laugh at those whom they had imposed upon. Such as these were ripe for ruin.
entries.d16268fc3bbe7021dda89a4c16b3a7e7007b9c03: <div eID="gen17364" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Destruction Threatened for Sin; Despair of Sinners in Trouble; The Prophet's Lamentation. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  606.)</title> <div sID="gen17365" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> I will surely consume them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree, and the leaf shall fade; and <hi type="italic">the things that</hi> I have given them shall pass away from them. <hi type="super">14</hi> Why do we sit still? assemble yourselves, and let us enter into the defenced cities, and let us be silent there: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God hath put us to silence, and given us water of gall to drink, because we have sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> We looked for peace, but no good <hi type="italic">came; and</hi> for a time of health, and behold trouble! <hi type="super">16</hi> The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan: the whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they are come, and have devoured the land, and all that is in it; the city, and those that dwell therein. <hi type="super">17</hi> For, behold, I will send serpents, cockatrices, among you, which <hi type="italic">will</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> charmed, and they shall bite you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">When</hi> I would comfort myself against sorrow, my heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> faint in me. <hi type="super">19</hi> Behold the voice of the cry of the daughter of my people because of them that dwell in a far country: <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in Zion? <hi type="italic">is</hi> not her king in her? Why have they provoked me to anger with their graven images, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with strange vanities? <hi type="super">20</hi> The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved. <hi type="super">21</hi> For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt; I am black; astonishment hath taken hold on me. <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> no balm in Gilead; <hi type="italic">is there</hi> no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered? <div eID="gen17365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17366" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen17366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17367" type="x-p"/> I. God threatening the destruction of a sinful people. He has borne long with them, but they are still more and more provoking, and therefore now their ruin is resolved on: <hi type="italic">I will surely consume them (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.13">v. 13</reference>), consuming I will consume them,</hi> not only surely, but utterly, consume them, will follow them with one judgment after another, till they are quite consumed; it is a <hi type="italic">consumption determined,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">Isa. x. 23</reference>. 1. They shall be quite stripped of all their comforts (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">There shall be no grapes on the vine.</hi> Some understand this as intimating their sin; God came looking for grapes from this vineyard, seeking fruit upon this fig-tree, but he <hi type="italic">found none</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Isa. v. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.6">Luke xiii. 6</reference>); nay, they had not so much as leaves, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.19">Matt. xxi. 19</reference>. But it is rather to be understood of God's judgments upon them, and may be meant literally—The enemy shall seize the fruits of the earth, shall pluck the grapes and figs for themselves and beat down the very leaves with them; or, rather, figuratively—They shall be deprived of all their comforts and shall have nothing left them wherewith to <hi type="italic">make glad their hearts.</hi> It is expounded in the last clause: <hi type="italic">The things that I have given them shall pass away from them.</hi> Note, God's gifts are upon condition, and revocable upon non-performance of the condition. Mercies abused are forfeited, and it is just with God to take the forfeiture. 2. They shall be set upon by all manner of grievances, and surrounded with calamities (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will send serpents among you,</hi> the Chaldean army, fiery serpents, flying serpents, cockatrices; these shall bite them with their venomous teeth, give them wounds that shall be mortal; and they <hi type="italic">shall not be charmed,</hi> as some serpents used to be, with music. These are serpents of another nature, that are not so wrought upon, or they are as <hi type="italic">the deaf adder, that stops her ear, and will not hear the voice of the charmer.</hi> The enemies are so intent upon making slaughter that it will be to no purpose to accost them gently, or offer any thing to pacify them, or mollify them, or to bring them to a better temper. No peace with God, therefore none with them. <div eID="gen17367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17368" type="x-p"/> II. The people sinking into despair under the pressure of those calamities. Those that were void of fear (when the trouble was at a distance) and set it at defiance, are void of hope now that it breaks in upon them, and have no heart either to make head against it or to bear up under it, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.14">v. 14</reference>. They cannot think themselves safe in the open villages: <hi type="italic">Why do we sit still here?</hi> Let us <hi type="italic">assemble, and go</hi> into a body <hi type="italic">into the defenced cities.</hi> Though they could expect no other than to be surely cut off there at last, yet not so soon as in the country, and therefore, "<hi type="italic">Let us go, and be silent there;</hi> let us attempt nothing, nor so much as make a complaint; for to what purpose?" It is not a submissive, but a sullen silence, that they here condemn themselves to. Those that are most jovial in their prosperity commonly despond most, and are most melancholy, in trouble. Now observe what it is that sinks them. <div eID="gen17368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17369" type="x-p"/> 1. They are sensible that God is angry with them: "<hi type="italic">The Lord our God has put us to silence,</hi> has struck us with astonishment, and <hi type="italic">given us water of gall to drink,</hi> which is both bitter and stupifying, or intoxicating. <reference osisRef="Ps.60.3">Ps. lx. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment.</hi> We had better sit still than rise up and fall; better say nothing than say nothing to the purpose. To what purpose is it to contend with our fate when God himself has become our enemy and fights against us? <hi type="italic">Because we have sinned against the Lord,</hi> therefore we are brought to the plunge." This may be taken as the language, (1.) Of their indignation. They seem to quarrel with God as if he had dealt hardly with them in putting them to silence, not permitting them to speak for themselves, and then telling them that it was because they had sinned against him. Thus men's foolishness <hi type="italic">perverts their way, and</hi> then <hi type="italic">their hearts fret against the Lord.</hi> Or rather, (2.) Of their convictions. At length they begin to see the hand of God lifted up against them, and stretched out in the calamities under which they are now groaning, and to own that they have provoked him to contend with them. Note, Sooner or later God will bring the most obstinate to acknowledge both his providence and his justice in all the troubles they are brought into, to see and say both that it is his hand and that he is righteous. <div eID="gen17369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17370" type="x-p"/> 2. They are sensible that the enemy is likely to be too hard for them, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.16">v. 16</reference>. They are soon apprehensive that it is to no purpose to make head against such a mighty force; they and their people are quite dispirited; and, when the courage of a nation is gone, their numbers will stand them in little stead. <hi type="italic">The snorting of the horses was heard from Dan,</hi> that is, the report of the formidable strength of their cavalry was soon carried all the nation over and every body <hi type="italic">trembled at the sound of the neighing of his steeds;</hi> for <hi type="italic">they have devoured the land and all that is in the city;</hi> both town and country are laid waste before them, not only the wealth, but the inhabitants, of both, <hi type="italic">those that dwell therein.</hi> Note, When God appears against us, every thing else that is against us appears very formidable; whereas, if he be for us, every thing appears very despicable, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom. viii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen17370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17371" type="x-p"/> 3. They are disappointed in their expectations of deliverance out of their troubles, as they had been surprised when their troubles came upon them; and this double disappointment very much aggravated their calamity. (1.) The trouble came when they little expected it (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">We looked for peace,</hi> the continuance of our peace, <hi type="italic">but no good came,</hi> no good news from abroad; we looked <hi type="italic">for a time of health</hi> and prosperity to our nation, but, <hi type="italic">behold, trouble,</hi> the alarms of war; for, as it follows (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">the noise of the</hi> enemies' <hi type="italic">horses was heard from Dan.</hi> Their false prophets had cried <hi type="italic">Peace, peace,</hi> to them, which made it the more terrible when the scene of war opened on a sudden. This complaint will occur again, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">ch. xiv. 19</reference>. (2.) The deliverance did not come when they had long expected it (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">The harvest is past, the summer is ended;</hi> that is, there is a great deal of time gone. Harvest and summer are parts of the year, and when they are gone the year draws towards a conclusion; so the meaning is, "One year passes after another, one campaign after another, and yet our affairs are in as bad a posture as ever they were; no relief comes, nor is any thing done towards it: <hi type="italic">We are not saved.</hi>" Nay, there is a great deal of opportunity lost, the season of action is over and slipped, the summer and harvest are gone, and a cold and melancholy winter succeeds. Note, The salvation of God's church and people often goes on very slowly, and God keeps his people long in the expectation of it, for wise and holy ends. Nay, they stand in their own light, and put a bar in their own door, and are not saved because they are not ready for salvation. <div eID="gen17371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17372" type="x-p"/> 4. They are deceived in those things which were their confidence and which they thought would have secured their peace to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The daughter of my people</hi> cries, cries aloud, <hi type="italic">because of those that dwell in a far country,</hi> because of the foreign enemy that invades them, that comes from a far country to take possession of ours; this occasions the cry; and what is the cry? It is this: <hi type="italic">Is not the Lord in Zion? Is not her king in her?</hi> These were the two things that they had all along buoyed up themselves with and depended upon, (1.) That they had among them the temple of God, and the tokens of his special presence with them. The common cant was, "<hi type="italic">Is not the Lord in Zion?</hi> What danger then need we fear?" And they held by this when the trouble was breaking in upon them. "Surely we shall do well enough, for have we not God among us?" But, when it grew to an extremity, it was an aggravation of their misery that they had thus flattered themselves. (2.) That they had the throne of the house of David. As they had a temple, so they had a monarchy, <hi type="italic">jure divino—by divine right: Is not Zion's king in her?</hi> And will not Zion's God protect Zion's king and his kingdom? Surely he will; but why does he not? "What" (say they) "has Zion neither a God nor a king to stand by her and help her, that she is thus run down and likely to be ruined?" This outcry of theirs reflects upon God, as if his power and promise were broken or weakened; and therefore he returns an answer to it immediately: <hi type="italic">Why have they provoked me to anger with their graven images?</hi> They quarrel with God as if he had dealt unkindly by them in forsaking them, whereas they by their idolatry had driven him from them; they have withdrawn from their allegiance to him, and so have thrown themselves out of this protection. They <hi type="italic">fret themselves, and curse their king and their God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.21">Isa. viii. 21</reference>), when it is their own sin that <hi type="italic">separates between them and God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.2">Isa. lix. 2</reference>); they <hi type="italic">feared not the Lord,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">what can a king do for them?</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.10.3">Hos. x. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen17372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17373" type="x-p"/> III. We have here the prophet himself bewailing the calamity and ruin of his people; for there were more of the lamentations of Jeremiah than those we find in the book that bears that title. Observe here, 1. How great his griefs were. He was an eyewitness of the desolations of his country, and saw those things which by the spirit of prophecy he had foreseen. In the foresight, much more in the sight, of them, he cries out, "<hi type="italic">My heart is faint in me,</hi> I sink, I die away at the consideration of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">When I would comfort myself against my sorrow,</hi> I do but labour in vain; nay, every attempt to alleviate the grief does but aggravate it." It is our wisdom and duty, under mournful events, to do what we can to <hi type="italic">comfort ourselves against our sorrow,</hi> by suggesting to ourselves such considerations as are proper to allay the grief and balance the grievance. But sometimes the sorrow is such that the more it is repressed the more strongly it recoils. This may sometimes be the case of very good men, as of the prophet here, whose soul refused to be comforted and fainted at the cordial, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.2-Ps.77.3">Ps. lxxvii. 2, 3</reference>. He tells us (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.21">v. 21</reference>) what was the matter: "It is <hi type="italic">for the hurt of the daughter of my people</hi> that <hi type="italic">I am</hi> thus <hi type="italic">hurt;</hi> it is for their sin, and the miseries they have brought upon themselves by it; it is for this that <hi type="italic">I am black,</hi> that I look black, that I go in black as mourners do, and that <hi type="italic">astonishment has taken hold on me,</hi> so that I know not what to do nor which way to turn." Note, The miseries of our country ought to be very much the grief of our souls. A gracious spirit will be a public spirit, a tender spirit, a mourning spirit. It becomes us to lament the miseries of our fellow-creatures, much more to lay to heart the calamities of our country, and especially of the church of God, to <hi type="italic">grieve for the affliction of Joseph.</hi> Jeremiah had prophesied the destruction of Jerusalem, and, though the truth of his prophecy was questioned, yet he did not rejoice in the proof of the truth of his prophecy was questioned, yet he did not rejoice in the proof of the truth of it by the accomplishment of it, preferring the welfare of his country before his own reputation. If Jerusalem had repented and been spared, he would have been far from fretting as Jonah did. Jeremiah had many enemies in Judah and Jerusalem, that hated, and reproached, and persecuted him; and in the judgments brought upon them God reckoned with them for it and pleaded his prophet's cause; yet he was far from rejoicing in it, so truly did he forgive his enemies and desire that God would forgive them. 2. How small his hopes were (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Is there no balm in Gilead</hi>—no medicine proper for a sick and dying kingdom? <hi type="italic">Is there no physician there</hi>—no skilful faithful hand to apply the medicine?" He looks upon the case to be deplorable and past relief. There is no balm in Gilead that can cure the disease of sin, no physician there that can restore the health of a nation quite overrun by such a foreign army as that of the Chaldeans. The desolations made are irreparable, and the disease has presently come to such a height that there is no checking it. Or <reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">this verse</reference> may be understood as laying all the blame of the incurableness of their disease upon themselves; and so the question must be answered affirmatively: <hi type="italic">Is there no balm in Gilead—no physician there?</hi> Yes, certainly there is; God is able to help and heal them, there is a sufficiency in him to redress all their grievances. Gilead was a place in their own land, not far off. They had among themselves God's law and his prophets, with the help of which they might have been brought to repentance, and their ruin might have been prevented. They had princes and priests, whose business it was to reform the nation and redress their grievances. What could have been done more than had been done for their recovery? <hi type="italic">Why then was not</hi> their health restored? Certainly it was not owing to God, but to themselves; it was not for want of balm and a physician, but because they would not admit the application nor submit to the methods of cure. The physician and physic were both ready, but the patient was wilful and irregular, would not be tied to rules, but must be humoured. Note, If sinners die of their wounds, their blood is upon their own heads. The blood of Christ is balm in Gilead, his Spirit is the physician there, both sufficient, all-sufficient, so that they might have been healed, but would not.  <chapter eID="Jer.8"/> <div eID="gen17373" type="x-p"/>

entries.e54ee60dae6c713e90a1f4e897e023000e5c0dbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9774"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.8.1-Jer.8.22">Jr 8:1-22</reference>. The Jew's Coming Punishment; Their Universal and Incurable Impenitence.</title> <div sID="gen17276" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9774"/>1. The victorious Babylonians were about to violate the sanctuaries of the dead in search of plunder; for ornaments, treasures, and insignia of royalty were usually buried with kings. Or rather, their purpose was to do the greatest dishonor to the dead (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Is 14:19</reference>). <div eID="gen17276" type="x-p"/>
entries.df81c895abb04a0978400847581b683c11914c6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9775"/><div sID="gen17277" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9775"/><hi type="bold">2. spread ... before the sun, &c.--</hi>retribution in kind. The very objects which received their idolatries shall unconcernedly witness their dishonor.<div eID="gen17277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loved ... served ... after ... walked ... sought ... worshipped--</hi>Words are accumulated, as if enough could not be said fully to express the mad fervor of their idolatry to the heavenly host (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>).<div eID="gen17278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor ... buried--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jr 22:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dung--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.9.22">Jr 9:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.10">Psa 83:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17280" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3750cd6596a68758a940bf2e533b1ba771f9662: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9776"/><div sID="gen17281" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9776"/>3. The survivors shall be still worse off than the dead (<reference osisRef="Job.3.21">Job 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.3.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.9.6">Re 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen17281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which remain in all the places--</hi>"in all places of them that remain, whither I ... that is, in all places whither I have driven them that remain [Maurer]. <div eID="gen17282" type="x-p"/>
entries.64af5310c16eb7fac76fa468b51b7e56d8f226e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9777"/><div sID="gen17283" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9777"/>4. "Is it not a natural instinct, that if one falls, he rises again; if one turns away (that is, wanders from the way), he will return to the point from which he wandered? Why then does not Jerusalem do so?" He plays on the double sense of return; literal and metaphorical (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jr 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.1">4:1</reference>). <div eID="gen17283" type="x-p"/>
entries.df5b15b36a5ff3f7a03fa5f8c4e16c90e972dece: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9778"/><div sID="gen17284" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9778"/><hi type="bold">5. slidden ... backsliding--</hi>rather, as the Hebrew is the same as in <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jr 8:4</reference>, to which this verse refers, "turned away with a perpetual turning away."<div eID="gen17284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perpetual--</hi>in contrast to the "arise" ("rise again," <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jr 8:4</reference>).<div eID="gen17285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">refuse to return--</hi>in contrast to, "shall he ... not return" (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jr 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>). <div eID="gen17286" type="x-p"/>
entries.2df60dce96b96b28eb7e4649895bca8116603e99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9779"/><div sID="gen17287" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9779"/><hi type="bold">6. spake not aright--</hi>that is, not so as penitently to confess that they acted wrong. Compare what follows.<div eID="gen17287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every one ... his course--</hi>The Keri reads "course," but the Chetib, "courses." "They persevere in the courses whatever they have once entered on." Their wicked ways were diversified.<div eID="gen17288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horse rusheth--</hi>literally, "pours himself forth," as water that has burst its embankment. The mad rapidity of the war horse is the point of comparison (<reference osisRef="Job.39.19-Job.39.25">Job 39:19-25</reference>). <div eID="gen17289" type="x-p"/>
entries.01cd691e9d591640e304da981625036e9fc895e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9780"/><div sID="gen17290" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9780"/>7. The instinct of the migratory birds leads them with unfailing regularity to return every spring from their winter abodes in summer climes (<reference osisRef="Song.2.12">So 2:12</reference>); but God's people will not return to Him even when the winter of His wrath is past, and He invites them back to the spring of His favor.<div eID="gen17290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the heaven--</hi>emphatical. The birds whose very element is the air, in which they are never at rest, yet show a steady sagacity, which God's people do not.<div eID="gen17291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">times--</hi>namely, of migrating, and of returning.<div eID="gen17292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my people--</hi>This honorable title aggravates the unnatural perversity of the Jews towards their God.<div eID="gen17293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know not, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.4">Jr 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Is 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen17294" type="x-p"/>
entries.0018fac5c1835fb8a909ba9bc8cba7dfbe1190e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9781"/><div sID="gen17295" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9781"/><hi type="bold">8. law ... with us--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.2.17">Ro 2:17</reference>). Possessing the law, on which they prided themselves, the Jews might have become the wisest of nations; but by their neglecting its precepts, the law became given "in vain," as far as they were concerned.<div eID="gen17295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scribes--</hi>copyists. "In vain" copies were multiplied. Maurer translates, "The false pen of the scribes hath converted it [the law] into a lie." See Margin, which agrees with Vulgate. <div eID="gen17296" type="x-p"/>
entries.252930e2df37e7fa24507a05aa830feabf1220e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9782"/><div sID="gen17297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9782"/><hi type="bold">9. dismayed--</hi>confounded.<div eID="gen17297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what wisdom--</hi>literally, "the wisdom of what?" that is, "wisdom in what respect?" the Word of the Lord being the only true source of wisdom (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.98-Ps.119.100">Psa 119:98-100</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pr 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.10">9:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17298" type="x-p"/>
entries.3472809861797c14a0de63e2fd67bae7b7c80d91: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9783"/><div sID="gen17299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9783"/>10-12. Repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.6.12-Jer.6.15">Jr 6:12-15</reference>. See a similar repetition, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.15">Jr 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">Jr 14:19</reference>.<div eID="gen17299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inherit--</hi>succeed to the possession of them. <div eID="gen17300" type="x-p"/>
entries.68ea1fbb72a1c9ef43c358590ca11bacad6a8683: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9785"/><div sID="gen17302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9785"/><hi type="bold">13. surely consume--</hi>literally, "gathering I will gather," or "consuming I will consume."<div eID="gen17302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no grapes ... nor figs--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Joel.1.7">Joe 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.19">Mt 21:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things that I have given ... shall pass away--</hi>rather, "I will appoint to them those who shall overwhelm (pass over) them," that is, I will send the enemy upon them [Maurer]. English Version accords well with the context; Though their grapes and figs ripen, they shall not be allowed to enjoy them. <div eID="gen17304" type="x-p"/>
entries.0662872dc2a741a7243bd555b6b32bf639e46e2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9786"/><div sID="gen17305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9786"/><hi type="bold">14. assemble--</hi>for defense.<div eID="gen17305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let us be silent--</hi>not assault the enemy, but merely defend ourselves in quiet, until the storm blow over.<div eID="gen17306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put us to silence--</hi>brought us to that state that we can no longer resist the foe; implying silent despair.<div eID="gen17307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">water of gall--</hi>literally, "water of the poisonous plant," perhaps the poppy (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.15">Jr 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.15">23:15</reference>). <div eID="gen17308" type="x-p"/>
entries.85bc81059858ecbc4c54b01e637adc8eb201a697: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9787"/><div sID="gen17309" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9787"/>15. Repeated (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">Jr 14:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We looked for--</hi>owing to the expectations held out by the false prophets.<div eID="gen17310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">health--</hi>healing; that is, restoration from adversity. <div eID="gen17311" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfcccfce775cd30724715602a2730aae2a0667f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9788"/><div sID="gen17312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9788"/><hi type="bold">16. his horses--</hi>the Chaldean's.<div eID="gen17312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was heard--</hi>the prophetical past for the future.<div eID="gen17313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Dan--</hi>bordering on Phoenicia. This was to be Nebuchadnezzar's route in invading Israel; the cavalry in advance of the infantry would scour the country.<div eID="gen17314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong ones--</hi>a poetical phrase for steeds, peculiar to Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.47.3">Jr 47:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jr 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.23">6:23</reference>). <div eID="gen17315" type="x-p"/>
entries.1386ccfecb93d180057e1b45dae533d7a5fe50b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9789"/><div sID="gen17316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9789"/><hi type="bold">17. I--</hi>Jehovah.<div eID="gen17316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cockatrices--</hi>basilisks (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.8">Is 11:8</reference>), that is, enemies whose destructive power no means, by persuasion or otherwise, can counteract. Serpent-charmers in the East entice serpents by music, and by a particular pressure on the neck render them incapable of darting (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.4">Psa 58:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen17317" type="x-p"/>
entries.49d259daa9a2fd9742bd263522b4846ed26ae59c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9790"/><div sID="gen17318" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9790"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.4">Is 22:4</reference>). The lamentation of the prophet for the impending calamity of his country.<div eID="gen17318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against sorrow--</hi>or, with respect to sorrow. Maurer translates, "Oh, my exhilaration as to sorrow!" that is, "Oh, that exhilaration ('comfort', from an Arabic root, to shine as the rising sun) would shine upon me as to my sorrow!"<div eID="gen17319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in me--</hi>within me. <div eID="gen17320" type="x-p"/>
entries.0074f23992033a14eec3af1a4b8c875407921f88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9791"/><div sID="gen17321" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9791"/>19. The prophet in vision hears the cry of the exiled Jews, wondering that God should have delivered them up to the enemy, seeing that He is Zion's king, dwelling in her (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>). In the latter half of the verse God replies that their own idolatry, not want of faithfulness on His part, is the cause.<div eID="gen17321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of them that dwell in a far country--</hi>rather, "from a land of distances," that is, a distant land (<reference osisRef="Isa.39.3">Is 39:3</reference>). English Version understands the cry to be of the Jews in their own land, because of the enemy coming from their far-off country.<div eID="gen17322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strange vanities--</hi>foreign gods. <div eID="gen17323" type="x-p"/>
entries.4b029ff37f59ccd703e70a5ec7d644d4353bc9f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9792"/><div sID="gen17324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9792"/>20. Proverbial. Meaning: One season of hope after another has passed, but the looked-for deliverance never came, and now all hope is gone. <div eID="gen17324" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2279c34f50bbafc711bc3c01646239300a1e623: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9793"/><div sID="gen17325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9793"/><hi type="bold">21. black--</hi>sad in visage with grief (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.6">Joe 2:6</reference>). <div eID="gen17325" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed329268d75f2dff9a907dcfd04a043fd9276741: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9794"/><div sID="gen17326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9794"/><hi type="bold">22. balm--</hi>balsam; to be applied to the wounds of my people. Brought into Judea first from Arabia Felix, by the queen of Sheba, in Solomon's time [Josephus, Antiquities, 8.2]. The opobalsamum of Pliny; or else [Bochart] the resin drawn from the terebinth. It abounded in Gilead, east of Jordan, where, in consequence, many "physicians" established themselves (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.11">Jr 46:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.8">51:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.37.25">Ge 37:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.11">43:11</reference>).<div eID="gen17326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">health ... recovered--</hi>The Hebrew is literally, "lengthening out ... gone up"; hence, the long bandage applied to bind up a wound. So the Arabic also [Gesenius]. <chapter eID="Jer.8"/>

entries.6b33c683041d685b350d0a444aee4896104c74ee: <div eID="gen29424" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29425" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29426" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29426" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29425" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29427" type="x-p"/> The judgments threatened in the last chapter are here declared to extend to the very dead, whose tombs should be opened, and the carcasses treated with every mark of indignity, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.1-Jer.8.3">Jer 8:1-3</reference>. From this the prophet returns to reprove them for their perseverance in transgression, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4-Jer.8.6">Jer 8:4-6</reference>; and for their thoughtless stupidity, which even the instinct of the brute creation, by a beautiful contrast, is made to upbraid, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7-Jer.8.9">Jer 8:7-9</reference>. This leads to farther threatening expressed in a variety of striking terms, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.10-Jer.8.13">Jer 8:10-13</reference>. Upon which a chorus of Jews is introduced, expressing their terror on the news of the invasion, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.14">Jer 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.15">Jer 8:15</reference>; which is greatly heightened in the neat verse by the prophet's hearing the snorting of Nebuchadnezzar's horses even from Dan, and then seeing the devastation made by his army, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.16">Jer 8:16</reference>, whose cruelties God himself declares no entreaties will soften, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.17">Jer 8:17</reference>. On this declaration the prophet laments most bitterly the fate of the daughter of his people, changing the scene unawares to the place of her captivity, where she is introduced answering in mournful responses to the prophet's dirge, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18-Jer.8.22">Jer 8:18-22</reference>. The variety of images and figures used to diversify the same subject is equally pleasing and astonishing. The dress is generally new, always elegant. <div eID="gen29427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29428" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29429" type="x-p"/> They shall bring out the bones - This and the two following verses are a continuation of the preceding prophecy, and should not have been separated from the foregoing chapter. <div eID="gen29429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29430" type="x-p"/> In order to pour the utmost contempt upon the land, the victorious enemies dragged out of their graves, caves, and sepulchers, the bones of kings, princes, prophets, priests, and the principal inhabitants, and exposed them in the open air; so that they became, in the order of God's judgments, a reproach to them in the vain confidence they had in the sun, moon, and the host of heaven - all the planets and stars, whose worship they had set up in opposition to that of Jehovah. This custom of raising the bodies of the dead, and scattering their bones about, seems to have been general. It was the highest expression of hatred and contempt. Horace refers to it: - <div eID="gen29430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29431" type="x-p"/> Barbarus, heu, cineres insistet victor, et urbem <div eID="gen29431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29432" type="x-p"/> Eques sonante verberabit ungula: <div eID="gen29432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29433" type="x-p"/> Quaeque carent ventis et solibus ossa Quirini (Nefas videre) dissipabit insolens. <div eID="gen29433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29434" type="x-p"/> Epod. 16:11. "Barbarians fell shall wanton with success, <div eID="gen29434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29435" type="x-p"/> Scatter the city's flaming ruins wide; <div eID="gen29435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29436" type="x-p"/> Or through her streets in vengeful triumph ride, <div eID="gen29436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29437" type="x-p"/> And her great founder's hallowed ashes spurn, <div eID="gen29437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29438" type="x-p"/> That slept uninjured in the sacred urn." <div eID="gen29438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29439" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen29439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29440" type="x-p"/> See this judgment referred to, Baruch 2:24, 25.
entries.38b7b365dcd269732fc416cb04584e518508da7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29441" type="x-p"/> Moreover thou shalt say - Dr. Blayney very properly observes, "In that part of the prophecy which follows next, the difference of speakers requires to be attended to; the transition being quick and sudden, but full of life and energy. The prophet at first, in the name of God, reproves the people's incorrigibility; he charges their wise ones with folly, and threatens them with grievous calamities, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4-Jer.8.13">Jer 8:4-13</reference>. In the three next verses he seems to apostrophize his countrymen in his own person, and as one of the people that dwelt in the open towns, advising those that were in the like situation to retire with him into some of the fortified cities, and there wait the event with patience, since there was nothing but terror abroad, and the noise of the enemy, who had already begun to ravage the country, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.14-Jer.8.16">Jer 8:14-16</reference>. God speaks, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.17">Jer 8:17</reference>, and threatens to bring foes against them that should be irresistible. The prophet appears again in his own person, commiserating the daughter of his people, who is heard bewailing her forlorn case in a distant land; while the voice of God, like that of conscience, breaks in upon her complaints, and shows her that all this ruin is brought upon her by her own infidelities, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18-Jer.8.20">Jer 8:18-20</reference>. The prophet once more resumes his discourse; he regrets that no remedy can be found to close up the wounds of his country, and pathetically weeps over the number of her slain, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.21">Jer 8:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jer 9:1</reference>." <div eID="gen29441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29442" type="x-p"/> Shall they fall, and not arise? shall he turn away, and not return? - That is, It is as possible for sinners to return from their sin to God, for his grace is ever at hand to assist, as it is for God, who is pouring out his judgments, to return to them on their return to him. But these held fast deceit, and refused to return; they would not be undeceived.
entries.1a3bd128df6e514b8ddbf35c386c0beda88a028a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29443" type="x-p"/> As the horse rusheth into the battle - This strongly marks the unthinking, careless desperation of their conduct.
entries.1eff569d4ce000a7c27a8bc974fed46a146823c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29444" type="x-p"/> The stork in the heaven - The birds of passage know the times of their going and return, and punctually observe them; they obey the dictates of nature, but my people do not obey my law.
entries.f754a068628c2a136a88a2d7aec20bd0c77843e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29445" type="x-p"/> The pen of the scribes is in vain - The deceitful pen of the scribes. They have written falsely, though they had the truth before them. It is too bold an assertion to say that "the Jews have never falsified the sacred oracles;" they have done it again and again. They have written falsities when they knew they were such.
entries.9e6acdd7bad052330ae345e8d09e428bfcaaee5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29446" type="x-p"/> Therefore will I give their wives - From this to the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.8.15">Jer 8:15</reference> is repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.6.13-Jer.6.15">Jer 6:13-15</reference>.
entries.a53f09aad907e3a99fa4ad2f29dac56f29e114fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29447" type="x-p"/> The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan - From this to the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.8.15">Jer 8:15</reference> is repeated from Babylon to Jerusalem; and it was by this city, after the battle of Carchemish, that Nebuchadnezzar, in pursuing the Egyptians, entered Palestine. <div eID="gen29447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29448" type="x-p"/> The whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones - Of his war horses. This is a fine image; so terrible was the united neighing of the cavalry of the Babylonians that the reverberation of the air caused the ground to tremble. This is better, and more majestic, than the celebrated line of Virgil: - <div eID="gen29448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29449" type="x-p"/> Quadrupe - dante pu - trem soni-tu quatit ungula campum. <div eID="gen29449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29450" type="x-p"/> It would be much easier to shake the ground with the prancings of many horses, than to cause an earthquake by the sound of the neighing of the troops of cavalry.
entries.d53506392737cf7eeeea8ac6966e3acb18c9389e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen29450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29451" type="x-p"/> I will send serpents - These were symbols of the enemies that were coming against them; a foe that would rather slay them and destroy the land than get booty and ransom.
entries.8958a43ad5fdd2ed6a7a2c1ee184d02e399abbc2: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29452" type="x-p"/> The harvest is past - The siege of Jerusalem lasted two years; for Nebuchadnezzar came against it in the ninth year of Zedekiah, and the city was taken in the eleventh; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1-2Kgs.25.3">2Kgs 25:1-3</reference>. This seems to have been a proverb: "We expected deliverance the first year - none came. We hoped for it the second year - we are disappointed; we are not saved - no deliverance is come."
entries.2d31d4215c37fea5f4fbffb086f169e436f1efc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen29452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29453" type="x-p"/> Is there no balm in Gilead? - Yes, the most excellent in the world. "Is there no physician there?" Yes, persons well skilled to apply it. "Why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?" Because ye have not applied to the physician, nor used the balm. Ye die because ye will not use the remedy. But to apply this metaphor: - The Israelites are represented as a man dying through disease; and a disease for the cure of which the balm of Gilead was well known to be a specific, when judiciously applied by a physician. But though there be balm and a physician, the people are not cured; neither their spiritual nor political evils are removed. But what may all this spiritually mean? The people are morally diseased; they have sinned against God, and provoked him to destroy them. They are warned by the prophet to repent and turn to God: they refuse, and sin on. Destruction is come upon them. Might they not have avoided it? Yes. Was it the fault of God? No. Did he not send his prophets with the richest offers of mercy? Did he not give them time, the best instructions, and the most effectual means of returning to him? Has not mercy, the heavenly balm, been ever at hand? And has not God, the great Physician, been ever ready to apply it? Yes. Why then are they not converted and healed? Because they would not apply to the Divine Physician, nor receive the only remedy by which they could be spiritually healed. They, then, that sin against the only remedy must perish, because they might have had it, but would not. It is not because there is a deficiency of grace, nor of the means of grace, that men are not saved; but because they either make no use, or a bad use, of them. Jesus Christ, by the grace of God, has tasted death for every man; but few are saved, because they Will Not come unto him that they may have life. <div eID="gen29453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29454" type="x-p"/> In my old MS. Bible the text is rendered thus: - <div eID="gen29454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29455" type="x-p"/> Whether gumm is not in Galaad? Or a leche is not there? Why than the hid wounde of the daughter of my peple is not all helid? <div eID="gen29455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29456" type="x-p"/> How shall they escape who neglect so great a salvation? Reader, lay this to heart; and, while there is time, apply heartily to the great Physician for thy cure.  <chapter eID="Jer.8"/> <div eID="gen29456" type="x-p"/>

entries.91526122f6c8ecc49c8ad3b492c6184f7e5b331a: <reference osisRef="Jer.8.1-Jer.8.2">Jer 8:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13906" type="x-p"/> But even then the judgment has not come to a height. Even sinners long dead must yet bear the shame of their sins. "At that time" points back to "days come" in Jer 7:32. The Masoretes wished to have the ו before יוציאוּ deleted, apparently because they took it for ו <hi type="italic">consec</hi>. But it here stands before the jussive, as it does frequently, e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.13.10">Jer 13:10</reference>, Exo 12:3. They will take the bones of the kings, princes, priests, and prophets, the rulers and leaders of the people (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.26">Jer 2:26</reference>), and the bones of the other inhabitants of Jerusalem, out of their graves, and spread them out before the sun, the moon, and the stars, i.e., expose them under the open sky to the influence of the heavenly bodies, so that they shall rot away, become "dung on the face of the earth." The worst dishonour that could be done to the dead, a just return in kind for their worship of sun, moon, and stars: cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.7.18">Exo 7:18</reference>; 2Ki 21:5; 2Ki 23:11. This worship the prophet describes in its various stages: "Inclination of the heart, the act of devoting and dedicating themselves to the service, the frequenting of gods’ sanctuary in order to worship and to obtain oracles; while he strives to bring out in strong relief the contrast between the zeal of their service and the reward they get by it" (Hitz.). They shall not be gathered, i.e., for burial: cf. 2Sa 21:13.; 1Sa 31:13. The dead shall suffer this at the hands of enemies despoiling the land. The reason for so doing was, as Jerome observes, the practice of burying ornaments and articles of value along with the dead. Seeking for such things, enemies will turn up the graves (cf. acts of this kind the case of Ibn Chaldun, in Sylv. de Sacy, <hi type="italic">Abdollat</hi>. p. 561), and, in their hatred and insolence, scatter the bones of the dead all about.
entries.c7d7e9bf61610ec560df80bf75fe8d6da7aaff39: <reference osisRef="Jer.8.3">Jer 8:3</reference> <div eID="gen13906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13907" type="x-p"/> Not less dreadful will be the fate of those who remain in life; so appalling that they will prefer death to life, since every kind of hardship in exile and imprisonment amongst the heathen is awaiting them: cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.36-Lev.26.39">Lev 26:36-39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.65">Deu 28:65</reference>-67. המּקמות  strikes us as peculiar, seeing that the latter word cannot be adjective to the former; for "in all the remaining places of Judah" (Umbr.) gives no suitable sense, and "in all remaining places outside of Judah" is contrary to usage. But הנּשׁארים may be taken as genitive, in spite of the article prefixed to the <hi type="italic">stat. constr</hi>. מקמות; and we may then translate, with Maur.: in all the places of those who remain whither I have driven them. The lxx have omitted the second word; and it is possible it may have found its way hither from the preceding line by an error of transcription. And so Hitz., Ew., and Graf have deleted it as a gloss; but the arguments adduced have little weight. The lxx have also omitted "and say to them," <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jer 8:4</reference>, have changed כּה into כּי, and generally have treated Jeremiah in a quite uncritical fashion: so that they may have omitted the word from the present verse because it seemed awkward to them, and was not found in the parallel passages, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.14">Jer 29:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jer 23:3</reference>, which are not, however, precisely similar to the present verse.
entries.21ba6aabb207b8ca8cf7a67306899356eff960ae: <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4-Jer.8.7">Jer 8:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen13907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13908" type="x-p"/> The People’s Obstinacy in Wickedness, and the Dreadfulness of the Judgment. - Since the people cleaves stedfastly to its sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.4-Jer.8.13">Jer 8:4-13</reference>), the Lord must punish sorely (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.14">Jer 8:14</reference> -23). - <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jer 8:4</reference>-13. <hi type="italic">"And say to them, Thus hath the Lord said: Doth one fall, and not rise again? or doth one turn away, and not turn back again?</hi> Jer 8:5. <hi type="italic">Why doth this people of Jerusalem turn itself away with a perpetual turning? They hold fast by deceit, they refuse to return.</hi> Jer 8:6. <hi type="italic">I listened and heard: they speak not aright; no one repenteth him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? They all turn to their course again, like a horse rushing into the battle.</hi> Jer 8:7. <hi type="italic">Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and turtle-dove, and swallow, and crane, keep the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of Jahveh.</hi> Jer 8:8. <hi type="italic">How can ye say, Wise are we, and the law of Jahve we have? Certainly the lying pen of the scribes hath made it a lie.</hi> Jer 8:9. <hi type="italic">Ashamed the wise men become, confounded and taken; lo, the word of Jahveh they spurn at; and whose wisdom have they?</hi> Jer 8:10. <hi type="italic">Therefore will I give their wives unto others, their fields to new heirs: for from the small to the great, they are all greedy for gain; from the prophet even unto the priest, they all use deceit.</hi> Jer 8:11. <hi type="italic">And they heal the hurt of the daughter of my people as it were a light matter, saying, Peace, peace; and yet there is no peace.</hi> Jer 8:12. <hi type="italic">They have been put to shame because they have done abomination; yet they take not shame to themselves, ashamedness they know not. Therefore they shall fall amongst them that fall: in the time of their visitation they shall stumble, that Jahve said.</hi> Jer 8:13. <hi type="italic">Away, away will I sweep them, saith Jahveh: no grapes on the vine, and no figs on the fig-tree, and the leaf is withered; so I appoint unto them those that shall pass over them."</hi> <div eID="gen13908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13909" type="x-p"/> This strophe connects itself with what precedes. A judgment, dreadful as has been described in <reference osisRef="Jer.7.32-Jer.8.3">Jer 7:32-8:3</reference>, will come on Judah, because the people cleaves stiffneckedly to its sins. The ואמרתּ of <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jer 8:4</reference> corresponds to that in Jer 7:28. The questioning clauses in <reference osisRef="Jer.8.4">Jer 8:4</reference> contain universal truths, which are applied to the people of Judah in Jer 8:5. The subjects to יפּלוּ and ישׁוּב are indefinite, hence singular and plural with like significance: cf. Gesen. §137, 3; Ew. §294, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The verb ישׁוּב, turn oneself, turn about, is here used in a double sense: first, as turn away from one; and then turn towards him, return again.
